facts.raw_span: A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use
altered mental status
febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10)
left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5)
leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL)
Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates
Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage
Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema
Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³
no valvular vegetations
Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³
Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement

concepts.why: The patient has altered mental status, fever, and CSF findings consistent with meningoencephalitis, including elevated WBCs and protein.
The patient has a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect on CT and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity on MRI, which could be consistent with vasculitis.
The patient has a history of intravenous heroin use and urine toxicology positive for benzodiazepines and opiates, which could contribute to toxic leukoencephalopathy.
The patient has a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect on CT and elevated WBCs in CSF, which could be consistent with a brain abscess.
The patient has altered mental status and fever, which could be consistent with encephalitis.
The patient has left upper- and lower-limb weakness and a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia on CT, which could be consistent with a stroke.
The patient has altered mental status and a history of intravenous heroin use, which could contribute to metabolic encephalopathy.
The patient has a history of hepatitis C and altered mental status, which could be consistent with hepatic encephalopathy.
The patient has fever, leukocytosis, and elevated WBCs in CSF, which could be consistent with a rickettsial infection.
The patient has a history of immunosuppression and MRI findings consistent with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

rationales.F01: Hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use may contribute to various neurological conditions, but the presence of these factors alone does not strongly rule in or out any of the listed concepts.
rationales.F03: Fever and altered mental status are nonspecific symptoms that can be seen in various conditions, including infections and inflammatory processes.
rationales.F06: The presence of benzodiazepines and opiates in urine toxicology may suggest toxic leukoencephalopathy or other substance-related conditions.
rationales.F09: The cerebrospinal fluid findings, including elevated white blood cell count and protein, are indicative of an inflammatory or infectious process, such as meningitis or encephalitis.
rationales.F11: The repeat lumbar puncture showing increased white blood cell count and protein suggests a worsening or persistent inflammatory or infectious process.
rationales.F12: The progression of MRI findings, including new involvement of the left basal ganglia and increased diffusion restriction, suggests a worsening or evolving condition, such as an infectious or inflammatory process.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with altered mental status, fever, and CSF findings (elevated WBCs, protein, and decreased glucose) supports Subacute Meningoencephalitis. The absence of valvular vegetations and negative cultures reduce the likelihood of other infectious causes. While Toxic Leukoencephalopathy is a consideration due to the patient's history of substance use and positive urine toxicology, the CSF findings and clinical progression are more consistent with Subacute Meningoencephalitis.
